text.en: Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.
text.th: Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

text.en: Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:
text.th: Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

text.en: "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."
text.th: "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

text.en: The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.
text.th: The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

text.en: We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.
text.th: We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

text.en: But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?
text.th: But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

text.en: This is the key idea behind decision models.
text.th: This is the key idea behind decision models.

text.en: What are decision models?
text.th: What are decision models?

text.en: A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.
text.th: A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

text.en: Why not use LLMs for everything?
text.th: Why not use LLMs for everything?

text.en: We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.
text.th: We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

text.en: However, there are a few problems with this approach.
text.th: However, there are a few problems with this approach.

text.en: LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices.
text.th: LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices.

text.en: Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work.
text.th: Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work.

text.en: Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work.
text.th: Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work.

text.en: How are decision models different from classification models?
text.th: How are decision models different from classification models?

text.en: Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.
text.th: Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

text.en: Traditional classification
text.th: Traditional classification

text.en: Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

text.en: A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.
text.th: A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

text.en: The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.
text.th: The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

text.en: If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.
text.th: If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

text.en: Zero-shot classification
text.th: Zero-shot classification

text.en: Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.
text.th: Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

text.en: Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

text.en: One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.
text.th: One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

text.en: This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

text.en: Where decision models differ
text.th: Where decision models differ

text.en: Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).
text.th: Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

text.en: More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.
text.th: More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

text.en: The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

text.en: Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem
text.th: Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem

text.en: Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.
text.th: Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

text.en: Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

text.en: Final thoughts
text.th: Final thoughts

text.en: Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.
text.th: Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

text.en: Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.
